summary: Describes a framework and process for developing performance metrics for protocols and applications carried over IETF protocols. Such metrics characterize traffic on live networks and services. It is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: Before measuring something with a ruler, everyone should agree what is being measured and how. This sets the rules for creating new, well-defined network measurements.

subtitle: A checklist and review process for anyone defining a new way to measure network or application performance.

tldr.problem: Performance measurements are only comparable if everyone defines and measures them the same way, but the IETF had a gap in coverage for metrics of protocols above and below the IP layer.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets out what a well-formed Performance Metric definition must contain, including six normative parts and four informative ones, and describes how proposals are reviewed with help from a Performance Metrics Directorate.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice for authors and reviewers of metric documents. It defines no metrics itself, and the text does not say it has been obsoleted.

today: RFC 6390 is a Best Current Practice published in October 2011, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a process and framework document, so it defines no metrics itself.

sections.title: Why Standard Metrics Matter
sections.content:
Networked applications are distributed, and their performance can be hurt by IP impairments, server capacity, congestion and other factors. Measuring that performance helps confirm that quality objectives are met and supports problem diagnosis. Standardized metrics keep measurement implementations consistent and make results easier to interpret and compare.

The RFC names at least three phases in developing performance standards: defining a metric and its units, specifying a method of measurement, and specifying the reporting format. It notes a gap in the coverage of IETF working groups: metrics for protocols above and below the IP layer that can characterize live networks. Earlier work such as RFC 4710 (RAQMON), RFC 3611 (RTCP XR) and RFC 6035 covers reporting, but not general metric development.

The audience is IETF participants who write metric documents, the reviewers of those documents, and members of the Performance Metrics Directorate.
sections.plainLanguage: If every school timed races with a different stopwatch and different rules, you could not compare scores. Standard metrics mean everybody times things the same way.

sections.title: Purpose, Scope and Key Terms
sections.content:
The document provides a framework and a process for metrics of protocols above and below the IP layer. It explicitly does not define any Performance Metrics. A Performance Metric is a quantitative measure of performance specific to an IETF-specified protocol, or to an application carried over one. Examples given are FTP response time for a complete file download and DNS response time to resolve an IP address.

It does not supersede existing working methods of chartered working groups, and it is not meant to govern groups that already focus on metrics, such as IPPM and BMWG, though it MAY be applied there. It covers metrics from both active and passive measurements.

The Performance Metrics Directorate is a directorate that gives guidance on metric development, and should be composed of experts potentially selected from the IPPM, BMWG and PMOL working groups.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a guide for writing measurement rules, not a list of measurements. It also names a small team of experts who help check the rules.

sections.title: QoS, QoE and Application Metrics
sections.content:
Quality of Service (QoS) is defined in the style of ITU E.800 as the totality of characteristics of a service that bear on its ability to satisfy stated and implied needs of the user. Quality of Experience (QoE) is the level of quality that users believe they have experienced, and it has a quantitative and a qualitative component.

Network QoS concerns network and protocol performance, while QoE assesses a user's experience in the context of a task. Application-specific metrics sit between them. For example, packet loss, delay and delay variation can be used to estimate de-jitter buffer size and RTP-layer loss, and then combined with facts like codec type to estimate a Mean Opinion Score.

QoS and application-specific metrics are quantitative, while QoE is qualitative. The same VoIP quality can feel different in a casual chat, a business conference call or an emergency call.
sections.plainLanguage: QoS is what the machines can measure, like how many letters got lost in the mail. QoE is how happy you felt about the mail service, which depends on what you needed the letter for.

sections.title: What Makes a Good Performance Metric
sections.content:
A metric measures an observable behavior of a technology, application or service. It is usually measured directly but may be computed, in which case it may estimate a parameter of an underlying statistical process. A metric should serve a defined purpose, such as measuring capacity, quantifying problems, checking service levels or locating faults.

The RFC lists four tests of usefulness: how much information would be lost without the metric, how well it correlates with QoS and QoE, how well it helps identify and locate problems, and whether policies such as a Service Level Agreement need to be based on it. Its worked example is Packet Loss Rate (PLR): if an application is sensitive to bursts of loss, a plain mean PLR correlates weakly, and a measure of the duration and frequency of periods when PLR exceeds a threshold may serve better.

Metrics can also be composed from base metrics by a deterministic function. Spatial composition combines metrics of one type across different spatial domains, temporal composition combines them across different time spans, and temporal aggregation summarizes many values into fewer, such as a minimum, maximum and average. An index is a metric whose output range was chosen for convenience, for example the R Factor.

Metric authors should also identify the audience, since it shapes the definition. Differences between users include passive versus active measurement, lab versus deployed networks, accuracy, access to measurement points, topology, scale, on-demand versus continuous measurement, reporting formats, sampling criteria, and measurement period.
sections.plainLanguage: A good measurement answers a real question and tells you something you would miss otherwise. Sometimes you build a new number out of smaller ones, like working out your average speed for a whole trip from each hour's speed.

sections.title: What a Metric Definition Must Contain
sections.content:
A definition MUST have a normative part saying what the metric is and how it is measured or computed, and it SHOULD have an informative part describing the metric and its application.

The normative part MUST define at least six things: the metric name (RECOMMENDED to be unique within its layer and context), the description, the method of measurement or calculation, the units, the measurement point(s) with any measurement domain, and the measurement timing. The method must say whether measurement is active or passive, qualify terms like average, and define exception cases. The classic trap is packet loss: a definition may not say when a late packet counts as lost rather than delayed, or how duplicates are handled.

The informative part SHOULD cover four things: implementation guidance so implementers get consistent results, verification advice such as test vectors, use and applications including typical and abnormal ranges and security implications, and the reporting model. The RFC gives a speech level example, where a typical range of -18 to -28 dBm0 makes a reading of -7 dBm0 understandable.

Section 5.4.5 applies the template to the loss rate metric of RFC 3611.
sections.plainLanguage: Every measurement needs a name, a plain description, step-by-step instructions, the unit, where you stand to measure, and how often. Extra pages explain how to use it and how to double-check your work.

sections.title: Dependencies, Results and Parameters
sections.content:
Metric designers should document hidden dependencies. Timing accuracy matters: for a metric such as events per time interval, a 10% variation in the interval gives a 10% variation in the measured value. Definitions may also rely on non-obvious factors, for instance recognizing a packet as lost needs a way to know it was lost (such as an RTP sequence number) and a time threshold.

Lower-layer metrics may be used to infer higher-layer application performance, and accuracy depends on the completeness of the metric set, the correlation between inputs and application performance, and variability. A middlebox such as a proxy, NAT, session border controller or application layer gateway can add variability to measurements or limit their scope.

Results may follow the IPPM organization of a singleton (one atomic value), a sample (a set of singletons) and a statistic (a value derived from a sample, such as the mean). Finally, documents SHOULD identify all key parameters, the variables left for the user to set and report, such as the scope, time of measurement, sliding-window length, timer settings and counter thresholds.
sections.plainLanguage: Things like a wobbly stopwatch or a gatekeeper who blocks your messenger can change your results, so a good rulebook points them out and says which settings you have to write down.

sections.title: The Development and Review Process
sections.content:
The process adds to the work-adoption rules of RFC 2026 and RFC 2418, and new metric work items SHALL still be approved through the existing IETF process. Proposals SHOULD be written as Internet-Drafts, SHOULD be deliverables of the relevant working group charter and vetted by that group first, SHOULD assess overlap with other standards bodies, SHOULD name the intended audience, and SHOULD identify security and IANA needs (for example a metrics registry).

Each metric SHOULD be reviewed against a list of questions. Is it unambiguously defined? Are units and the measurement interval specified? Are significant sources of error identified? Are results repeatable and the metric implementable? Are there undocumented assumptions? Can results be related to application performance or user experience? Do the security considerations address denial of service, interference and user data confidentiality?

The Directorate SHALL provide guidance to the related working group. A formal review is recommended by the time the Area Directors review the document or an IETF Last Call is under way. Existing mailing lists SHOULD be used, and the Directorate also helps with progress along the Standards Track, such as preparing test plans for different implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: A new measurement idea is written up, checked by the group that cares most about it, and then looked over by the experts, who run through a list of questions like "is it clear?" and "can someone repeat it and get the same answer?".

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: A framework for metric development is not itself a security issue, but individual metric definitions may be. The RFC recommends that people defining metrics identify any such risk factors. Security considerations that apply to active measurement of live networks (see RFC 4656) and to passive measurement of specific packets (see RFC 5475) are relevant. Earlier in the text, the risks named are revealing data that identifies a user and misuse of active test tools.
sections.plainLanguage: Measuring can accidentally reveal private things about people or be abused to flood a network, so anyone inventing a measurement should think about that first.
